explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says, "…if your heart is wise, my own heart will indeed rejoice." Not a fat bank account or a big title, just a wise heart. I think any dad would take that deal, and I would too.

Fields sound like a fair guess, friend, because a big harvest feels like something a dad would brag about. But the writer never mentions land. What makes his heart rejoice is his son's wise heart. A huge field with a foolish heart standing in it is just more room to make mistakes.

Fame is a fun guess, friend, but the verse never says a word about it. The writer says, "…if your heart is wise, my own heart will indeed rejoice." Wise comes first. Nobody has to know your name for your heart to be wise.

Lips it is. The writer says, "My inmost being will rejoice when your lips speak what is right." That's joy way down deep, not a polite clap. Notice what comes right after the wise heart in verse 15: right words coming out of the mouth.

Friends are a nice thought, baker, but the verse says lips. The writer says his inmost being will rejoice when "…your lips speak what is right." Friends can cheer from the sidelines, but the lips in this verse belong to the son.
Elders don't show up in this verse, friend. The writer's inmost being rejoices when his son's own lips speak what is right. The son does the talking here. Nobody is handing him a script.

You got it, baker. The writer says, "Do not let your heart envy sinners, but always continue in the fear of the LORD." When your eyes drift over to somebody else's lucky streak, he points them back to the LORD. And he says always, not just on the easy days.

The king never comes up in this verse, friend. The writer says to "…always continue in the fear of the LORD." That's where he wants his son's heart to stay planted. Chasing a king's favor is a whole different job.

Riches are a tempting guess, baker, but the verse doesn't go there. When the writer warns against envying sinners, he says to "…always continue in the fear of the LORD." Nothing about chasing a bigger pile. I think that's a lot less tiring than the pursuit of riches, honestly.

It's the other way around, baker. The writer says, "For surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off." So the card has it backwards. Just before that, he tells his son to always continue in the fear of the LORD.

That's right, friend. The writer says, "For surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off." The card flips it around. Just before that, he tells his son to always continue in the fear of the LORD.

Right on, baker. The writer says, "Do not join those who drink too much wine or gorge themselves on meat." He's talking about the crowd, not just the cup. I'm a cookie stamper and even I know that two dozen cookies in one sitting never ends well.

Close, friend, but the verse says it plainly: "Do not join those who drink too much wine or gorge themselves on meat." He tells his son to keep out of that crowd. So the statement on the card is true, not false.

Poverty, baker. The writer says, "For the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty…" The crowd he warned about in verse 20 is the crowd that poverty is coming for. And he's not done, because drowsiness gets a say too.

Honor would be a nice ending, friend, but the verse goes the other direction. The writer says the drunkard and the glutton "…will come to poverty…" It's a warning, and honor isn't what's waiting at the end of it.

Power sounds like a fun ending, baker, but that's not what the writer says. He says the drunkard and the glutton "…will come to poverty…" Nothing in the verse puts them in charge of anything. It points to the empty end.

explanations.answer: Do not despise her when she is old
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says, "Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old." The word old matters there. Respect for her doesn't expire when her hair turns gray.

explanations.answer: Do not leave her when you marry
explanations.explanation: Marriage never comes up in this verse, friend. The writer says, "…do not despise your mother when she is old." It's about how the son treats her as the years go by. Leaving or staying isn't what the verse is talking about.

explanations.answer: Do not argue with her at the gate
explanations.explanation: A gate scene would make a good movie, baker, but it's not in this verse. The writer says, "…do not despise your mother when she is old." That's the whole instruction about her. No gate, no arguing, just a warning against despising.

Sell is the word, baker. The writer says, "Invest in truth and never sell it…" Invest means you put something in and keep it. Truth, wisdom, instruction and understanding are not things to put up for sale.

Share sounds nice, friend, but that's not the verse. The writer says, "Invest in truth and never sell it…" He's talking about not trading truth away. Nothing in this verse tells anyone to keep it to themselves.

Test is a reasonable guess, baker, but the verse doesn't use it. The writer says, "Invest in truth and never sell it…" It's about holding on to truth, along with wisdom, instruction and understanding. Selling is the thing he rules out.

explanations.answer: The mother who gave him birth
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says, "May your father and mother be glad, and may she who gave you birth rejoice!" Verse 24 just before it speaks of a father rejoicing, and here the wish covers both parents. Mom is in it too.

explanations.answer: The friends who stood by him
explanations.explanation: Friends are good people to have, baker, but they're not named here. The writer says, "May your father and mother be glad, and may she who gave you birth rejoice!" The wish stays inside the family. Mom is the one he adds.

Elders aren't in this verse, friend. The writer says, "May your father and mother be glad, and may she who gave you birth rejoice!" After wishing joy on the father, he adds the mother. She's the one who gave birth to the son.

That's right, baker. The writer says, "For a prostitute is a deep pit, and an adulteress is a narrow well." I think this part is heavy, so I'll keep it short. The pictures are a pit that's deep and a well that's narrow.
Not this time, friend. The writer says, "For a prostitute is a deep pit, and an adulteress is a narrow well." So the card is true, word for word. It's a heavy warning, and he doesn't soften it.

That's the word, baker. The writer says, "Like a robber she lies in wait and multiplies the faithless among men." She's pictured like a robber lying in wait. What grows in number is the faithless among men.

Wise isn't the word here, friend. The writer says she "…multiplies the faithless among men." She's pictured like a robber lying in wait. What grows in number is the faithless, so that's the word that fits.
Wealthy is a fair guess, baker, but money isn't in this verse. The writer says she "…multiplies the faithless among men." She's pictured like a robber lying in wait. The word is faithless.

Wine is right, baker. The writer asks who has woe, sorrow and bloodshot eyes, then answers, "Those who linger over wine, who go to taste mixed drinks." The word linger is doing a lot of work there. These are the people who stay put and keep going back for more.

Riches would be an interesting answer, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. After the six questions, the writer answers, "Those who linger over wine, who go to taste mixed drinks." Wine is the answer, not a big bank account. Bloodshot eyes are the last of the six questions he asks.

Grudges can make a person miserable, baker, but that's not what the writer says here. He answers his own questions with, "Those who linger over wine, who go to taste mixed drinks." So the answer is wine. Not a grudge in sight.

It's the other way around, baker. The writer says, "Do not gaze at wine while it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly." The sparkle is exactly what he's warning about. The card flips the command, so it's false.

Yes, friend. The writer says, "Do not gaze at wine while it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly." He lists the red color, the sparkle and the smooth drink, then says don't gaze. So the card gets it backward.
That's the one, baker. The writer says, "In the end it bites like a snake and stings like a viper." It goes down smooth, but the end is the snake. A snake bite you don't see coming is the worst kind.

Fire is a good guess, friend, but the writer picks a different animal. He says, "In the end it bites like a snake and stings like a viper." The image is a snake, not a flame. It's a bite that comes after the smooth part.

A stone sinking is a strong picture, baker, but it's not the one in the verse. The writer says, "In the end it bites like a snake and stings like a viper." Wine gets a snake that bites and a viper that stings. And he puts it at the end.

Strange is right, baker. The writer says, "Your eyes will see strange things, and your mind will utter perversities." So it's the eyes and the mind that go off track. The writer pairs what he sees with what he says.

Holy isn't the word here, friend. The writer says, "Your eyes will see strange things, and your mind will utter perversities." What the drinker sees is strange, and what comes out of his mind is perversities. Nothing holy in that picture.

Beautiful is how the wine looked in verse 31, baker, red and sparkling. But in verse 33 the writer says the eyes will see "strange things." The full line is, "Your eyes will see strange things, and your mind will utter perversities."

That one's the opposite, baker. The writer says, "You will be like one sleeping on the high seas or lying on the top of a mast…" That's a pretty unsafe place to sleep. A cozy bed is nowhere in the picture.

You've got it, friend. The writer says, "You will be like one sleeping on the high seas or lying on the top of a mast…" Both of those are unsteady, high or tossing places. Nobody is safe in bed in this picture.

That's what the text says, baker. The drinker asks, "When can I wake up to search for another drink?" I think this one is sad, because he was beaten and didn't know it, and he still asks about another drink. The passage ends on that question.

explanations.answer: Find the men who hit him
explanations.explanation: Going after whoever hit him would make sense, friend, but that's not what he says. He says, "They struck me, but I feel no pain! They beat me, but I did not know it!" Then he asks, "When can I wake up to search for another drink?" The drink is what he asks about.

I'd love to hear that ending, baker, but the drinker doesn't say it. He asks, "When can I wake up to search for another drink?" I think that's the sad part. The only thing he asks about is another drink, not getting out.
